extracted.intended_audience: general public, global health students, policy makers, donors, and researchers interested in vaccine financing and global immunisation programs
extracted.subtask_description: Summary and evaluative description of Gavi (the Vaccine Alliance)'s funding mechanisms, program objectives (market-shaping, AMCs, HSS), measurement practices, and criticisms relevant to grant-funding and vaccine procurement. Useful for analysis of grant design, donor policy, and program accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-year funding cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: Gavi runs in five-year funding cycles which enables it to negotiate long-term deals with vaccine manufacturers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to secure long-term purchase commitments and stable deals with manufacturers; underpins budgeting and negotiation strategies for successive funding periods (examples: 2016–2020, 2021–2025, 2026–2030).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance Market Commitments (AMCs)
rubrics_metrics.description: AMCs aim to overcome market failure by making an advance pledge that if a vaccine for a certain condition is developed, meeting certain specifications, donors will buy a certain number of doses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed to encourage a competitive market and new vaccine development; examples include the pneumococcal vaccine AMC (subsidies to GSK and Pfizer, later price reductions via Serum Institute of India). Criticisms include transfer of subsidies to large incumbents and concerns about pricing and supplier diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic objective: 'shape the market for vaccines and other immunisation supplies'
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2011 Gavi added 'shape the market for vaccines and other immunisation supplies' to its strategic goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalised via long-term programs (e.g., 15-year pentavalent market program) intended to increase the number of certified manufacturers, increase competition, reduce price discrimination, and achieve lower prices and greater supply stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of Health Systems Strengthening (HSS) by vaccination coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Gavi measured HSS using vaccination coverage as the sole indicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice has been criticised as narrow and problematic: it creates a heavy accounting burden, may divert attention from countries' indigenous indicators, and may fail to capture broader HSS outcomes (e.g., operational research, policy development).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting indicators required of grant recipients
rubrics_metrics.description: Gavi set the reporting indicators which were required of recipients of its funding; countries were not allowed to use similar indicators they already collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticised for imposing a heavy accounting/reporting burden on recipients and for potentially undermining local measurement systems and priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: HSS funding allocation practice (short-term purchases vs long-term system strengthening)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses found just over half of sampled Gavi grant money went to purchasing drugs, equipment, supplies, and facilities (with small percentages on bonuses); WHO does not consider these short-term purchases to be HSS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques note lack of spending on operational research, improving use of existing resources, or developing national drug and vaccine policies; some grants used HSS funds for day-to-day operational costs without exit plans — implying a criterion that HSS funding should prioritize sustainable system investments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift HSS focus to sustainability and Paris Declaration principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Gavi subsequently shifted HSS aid to focus more on sustainability and the principles of the Paris Declaration for Aid Effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates an operational criterion: HSS grants should emphasize sustainability, country ownership, alignment and coordination consistent with Paris Declaration principles, and avoid one-off operational expenditures without sustainability/exit planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritisation of vaccine types (new expensive vaccines vs old low-cost vaccines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that Gavi focused on funding expensive new vaccines while putting less money and effort into expanding coverage of old, cheap ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by critics (e.g., MSF) to argue for a criterion that funding strategies should balance introduction of new vaccines with efforts to increase basic vaccine coverage among the unvaccinated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest and donor power in governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Gavi has been criticised for giving private donors more unilateral power to decide on global health goals and for conflicts of interest in having vaccine manufacturers on its governance board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggests governance/ethics criteria for grant-making bodies: manage conflicts of interest, ensure balanced donor influence, and maintain transparent decision-making to avoid undue private-sector control over priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on immunisation-specific HSS activities (cold chains)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gavi's HSS support tended to focus on immunisation strengthening support, especially the building of cold chains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates a practical criterion for HSS grant design: prioritize components that directly enable vaccine delivery (logistics, cold chain, staff training), while also monitoring whether such investments translate into sustained system improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditionality of platform/funding on meeting vaccine coverage goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Gavi's funding for the joint-venture Health Systems Funding Platform was conditional on the platform meeting vaccine coverage goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates use of performance conditionality in grant funding — funding tied to specific coverage metrics — and the trade-offs that creates with respect to recipient autonomy and measurement burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market-shaping justification: large, stable, high-volume deals to lower prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Gavi argued that low prices required large, stable, high-volume deals, and 'careful consideration and the support of key constituencies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a criterion for procurement strategy: use pooled/volume purchasing and long-term commitments to reduce prices, but balance that against risks of concentrating subsidies or supplier power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for quantifiable, election-cycle results
rubrics_metrics.description: Gavi programmes may produce quantified results within an election cycle, which is appealing to parties locked in an election cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies an implicit performance criterion: preference for programs that deliver measurable short-term outputs (e.g., immunisation coverage increases), which can bias funding toward interventions with rapid measurable impact rather than longer-term systemic change.
